title: 16 अक्टूबर के लिए मौसम का पूर्वानुमान: उत्तरी वियतनाम में तापमान बढ़ेगा, हनोई में भीषण गर्मी पड़ेगी और तापमान 34 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच जाएगा। - Vietnam.vn

full_text:
16 अक्टूबर के लिए मौसम का पूर्वानुमान: उत्तरी वियतनाम में तापमान बढ़ेगा, हनोई में भीषण गर्मी पड़ेगी और तापमान 34 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच जाएगा।
16 अक्टूबर को उत्तरी क्षेत्र में मौसम धूप वाला रहेगा, कुछ क्षेत्रों में तापमान 34 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच सकता है, जबकि दक्षिणी क्षेत्र में देर दोपहर और शाम को छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है।
राष्ट्रीय मौसम विज्ञान एवं जल विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान केंद्र के अनुसार, 16 अक्टूबर को दिन और रात दोनों समय, उत्तरी क्षेत्र और थान्ह होआ से ह्यू तक के प्रांतों में आमतौर पर धूप खिली रहेगी, हालांकि कुछ क्षेत्रों में सुबह तड़के कोहरा छा सकता है। वहीं, दक्षिण मध्य क्षेत्र, मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी क्षेत्र में दोपहर और शाम के बाद छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी, और कुछ क्षेत्रों में भारी बारिश भी हो सकती है।
अन्य क्षेत्रों में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी; विशेष रूप से दक्षिण और लाम डोंग में, दोपहर और शाम के दौरान छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी, और कुछ क्षेत्रों में भारी बारिश होगी।
पूर्वानुमानों के अनुसार, 16 अक्टूबर को दिन और रात दोनों समय, दक्षिणी क्षेत्र और लाम डोंग प्रांत में छिटपुट बौछारें और गरज के साथ बारिश होगी, जिसमें 10-30 मिमी तक वर्षा होगी, और कुछ स्थानों पर 70 मिमी से अधिक भारी बारिश भी हो सकती है (बारिश दोपहर और शाम के समय केंद्रित रहेगी)।
कृपया ध्यान दें कि बवंडर, बिजली, ओलावृष्टि और तेज हवाओं के झोंकों के साथ आने वाले तूफान कृषि उत्पादन को प्रभावित कर सकते हैं, पेड़ों को गिरा सकते हैं, घरों, परिवहन बुनियादी ढांचे और अन्य सुविधाओं को नुकसान पहुंचा सकते हैं।
विशेष रूप से, स्थानीय स्तर पर भारी वर्षा से छोटी नदियों और नालों में अचानक बाढ़, ढलानों पर भूस्खलन और निचले इलाकों में जलभराव होने की संभावना है।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है

हनोई: सुबह-सुबह कुछ इलाकों में कोहरा रहेगा, दिन में धूप खिली रहेगी, रात में बारिश नहीं होगी। हल्की हवा चलेगी। न्यूनतम तापमान 25-27 डिग्री सेल्सियस और अधिकतम तापमान 32-34 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा।
उत्तर-पश्चिमी क्षेत्र: छिटपुट बारिश, सुबह तड़के कुछ कोहरा, दिन में धूप खिली रहेगी। हल्की हवा चलेगी। न्यूनतम तापमान 20-23 डिग्री सेल्सियस, कुछ स्थानों पर 19 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे; अधिकतम तापमान 31-34 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा।
पूर्वोत्तर वियतनाम : सुबह-सुबह कुछ इलाकों में कोहरा, दिन में धूप, रात में हल्की बारिश। हल्की हवाएं। न्यूनतम तापमान 23-26 डिग्री सेल्सियस, पहाड़ी इलाकों में 22 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे; अधिकतम तापमान 31-34 डिग्री सेल्सियस।
थान्ह होआ से ह्यू तक: सुबह-सुबह कुछ क्षेत्रों में कोहरा, दिन में धूप, रात में छिटपुट बारिश। हल्की हवा। न्यूनतम तापमान 22-25 डिग्री सेल्सियस, अधिकतम तापमान 30-33 डिग्री सेल्सियस।
दक्षिण मध्य तट: दिन में धूप खिली रहेगी; शाम और रात में कुछ क्षेत्रों में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आ सकता है, विशेषकर दक्षिणी भाग में जहां कुछ स्थानों पर छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आएगा। उत्तर-पूर्वी हवा 2-3 स्तर की रहेगी। न्यूनतम तापमान 24-27 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा, कुछ स्थानों पर 24 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे भी जा सकता है; अधिकतम तापमान 29-32 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा, कुछ स्थानों पर 32 डिग्री सेल्सियस से ऊपर भी जा सकता है।

title: किशनगंज में भीषण गर्मी: तापमान 33°C तक, उमस से हाल बेहाल - Prabhat Khabar

full_text:
किशनगंज में गर्मी और उमस का असर, 33 डिग्री तक पहुंच सकता है अधिकतम तापमान
आसमान | Prabhat Khabar Network
किशनगंज में आज अधिकतम तापमान 33°C तक जा सकता है, जिससे गर्मी और उमस का एहसास होगा. मौसम विभाग ने खास सलाह दी है.
किशनगंज : जिले में शुक्रवार को सुबह हल्की धुंध के बाद दिन चढ़ने के साथ गर्मी बढ़ने की संभावना है. मौसम पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, अधिकतम तापमान 31 से 33 डिग्री सेल्सियस और न्यूनतम तापमान करीब 22 डिग्री रह सकता है. सुबह हवा में नमी रहने के कारण लोगों को उमस का एहसास हो सकता है.
दिन में तेज धूप से बढ़ेगी गर्मी
सुबह के बाद आसमान साफ होने और धूप तेज होने से दिन के तापमान में बढ़ोतरी महसूस हो सकती है. ऐसे में दोपहर के समय बाहर निकलने वाले लोगों को गर्मी और उमस का सामना करना पड़ सकता है.
सातों प्रखंडों में मौसम पर रहेगी नजर
बहादुरगंज, ठाकुरगंज, पोठिया, दिघलबैंक, टेढ़ागाछ, कोचाधामन और किशनगंज प्रखंड में स्थानीय परिस्थितियों के कारण मौसम में अंतर हो सकता है. फिलहाल सभी सात प्रखंडों के लिए अलग-अलग बारिश का पुख्ता पूर्वानुमान उपलब्ध नहीं है. ऐसे में बारिश या किसी अन्य मौसमी बदलाव को लेकर आधिकारिक मौसम अपडेट पर नजर रखना जरूरी है.

title: अक्टूबर में तापमान के 59 रिकॉर्ड बने; इस वर्ष, शीत मोर्चों की सक्रियता कम रही। - Vietnam.vn
search_term: ("पारा चढ़ा" OR "पारा पहुंचा" OR तापमान OR "तापमान बढ़ा" OR "रिकॉर्ड तोड़ गर्मी" OR "डिग्री सेल्सियस" OR "पारा उबला" OR "अधिकतम तापमान" OR "तापमान 40 पार" OR "तापमान 45 पार" OR "तापमान बढ़ने की संभावना") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
full_text:
अक्टूबर में तापमान के 59 रिकॉर्ड बने; इस वर्ष, शीत मोर्चों की सक्रियता कम रही।
(डैन त्रि अखबार) - अक्टूबर में, मौसम विज्ञान एजेंसियों ने 59 मौसम स्टेशनों पर दैनिक उच्चतम तापमान को उसी अवधि के ऐतिहासिक मूल्यों तक पहुंचने या उससे अधिक होने का रिकॉर्ड दर्ज किया।
राष्ट्रीय मौसम विज्ञान और जल विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान केंद्र के जलवायु पूर्वानुमान विभाग की मौसम पूर्वानुमानकर्ता ता थी होंग आन ने 2026 के अंतिम महीनों और 2027 की शुरुआत में अल नीनो के विकास और वियतनाम के मौसम और जलवायु पर इसके संभावित प्रभाव का पूर्वानुमान लगाया है।
सुश्री एन के अनुसार, अल नीनो बहुत मजबूत है, और यह अनुमान लगाया गया है कि अब से लेकर 2027 के पहले कुछ महीनों तक, यह घटना अपनी चरम तीव्रता पर पहुंच जाएगी, और फिर 2027 की गर्मियों की शुरुआत तक जारी रहेगी।
विशेषज्ञ ने बताया कि अल नीनो का प्रभाव तब स्पष्ट हुआ जब सितंबर और अक्टूबर के पहले पखवाड़े के दौरान, देश भर में तापमान आम तौर पर कई वर्षों के औसत से 1-2 डिग्री सेल्सियस अधिक रहा। विशेष रूप से, मौसम विज्ञान एजेंसी ने 59 मौसम स्टेशनों पर दैनिक अधिकतम तापमान को इसी अवधि के ऐतिहासिक मूल्यों के बराबर या उससे अधिक दर्ज किया।
उत्तर में, येन चाऊ मौसम स्टेशन (सोन ला प्रांत) ने 3 अक्टूबर को 38.3 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापमान दर्ज किया, जो 23 अक्टूबर, 2019 को दर्ज किए गए 37.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक था। हनोई में लैंग मौसम स्टेशन ने 2 अक्टूबर को 37.1 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापमान दर्ज किया, जो 5 अक्टूबर, 2023 को दर्ज किए गए पिछले रिकॉर्ड 36.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस को पार कर गया।
माई चाऊ ( फू थो ) में 1 अक्टूबर को तापमान 37.3 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गया, जो 11 अक्टूबर, 2003 को दर्ज किए गए 37.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक था। ची ने स्टेशन (फू थो) पर भी 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापमान दर्ज किया गया, जो 2003 में उसी दिन के पिछले रिकॉर्ड 35.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक था।
मुओंग ते ( लाई चाऊ ) में 2 अक्टूबर को तापमान 38 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गया, जो 19 अक्टूबर, 1991 को दर्ज किए गए 37.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस के रिकॉर्ड को पार कर गया। कई इलाकों में पिछले रिकॉर्ड की तुलना में तापमान में उल्लेखनीय वृद्धि दर्ज की गई।
मध्य और दक्षिणी वियतनाम में भी रिकॉर्ड तापमान दर्ज किया गया। 4 अक्टूबर को तुयेन होआ (क्वांग त्रि) मौसम स्टेशन पर 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापमान दर्ज किया गया, जो 12 अक्टूबर, 2003 के 36.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस के रिकॉर्ड को पार कर गया; बिएन होआ ( डोंग नाई ) में 1 अक्टूबर को तापमान 36.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गया, जो 19 अक्टूबर, 2025 के पिछले रिकॉर्ड 35.9 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक था।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
सुश्री एन ने भविष्यवाणी की कि नवंबर में, देश भर में औसत तापमान कई वर्षों के औसत से 1-2 डिग्री सेल्सियस अधिक रहेगा। इस वर्ष दिसंबर और जनवरी 2027 में, तापमान आमतौर पर कई वर्षों के औसत से 0.5-1.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस अधिक रहने की उम्मीद है, जिसमें मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी क्षेत्रों में 1-2 डिग्री सेल्सियस का अंतर रहने का अनुमान है।
विशेषज्ञों के अनुसार, उच्च तापमान के कारण इस सर्दी में ठंडी हवा का झोंका सामान्य से कमजोर हो रहा है, जिसका अर्थ है कि भीषण ठंड की लहरें बाद में आने की संभावना है, और उत्तरी और उत्तर मध्य वियतनाम में भीषण ठंड वाले दिनों की संख्या पिछले वर्षों की तुलना में कम होगी।
हालांकि, मौसम विज्ञान एजेंसी ने कहा कि स्थानीय स्तर पर भीषण ठंड और पाले की संभावना से इनकार नहीं किया जा सकता है।
इसके अलावा, मौसम विज्ञान एजेंसी के अनुसार, 2027 की वसंत ऋतु में हल्की बारिश और बूंदाबांदी कई वर्षों के औसत से कम होगी।
तूफानों और उष्णकटिबंधीय निम्न दबावों की स्थिति के बारे में सुश्री आन ने कहा कि अब से अक्टूबर के अंत तक पूर्वी सागर में इन मौसम प्रणालियों के प्रकट होने के कोई संकेत नहीं हैं। अगले वर्ष नवंबर से जनवरी के बीच पूर्वी सागर में लगभग 1-2 तूफान या उष्णकटिबंधीय निम्न दबाव आने की संभावना है, जिनका वियतनाम की मुख्य भूमि पर सीधा प्रभाव पड़ने की संभावना नहीं है।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
विशेषज्ञ ने यह भी कहा कि तापमान में वृद्धि के साथ-साथ अल नीनो के कारण बारिश और पानी की कमी का खतरा बढ़ जाता है। 2026 के शेष महीनों में मध्य क्षेत्र में बारिश का स्तर पिछले कई वर्षों के औसत से कम रहने का अनुमान है; मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी वियतनाम में भी बारिश का मौसम सामान्य से पहले समाप्त होने की संभावना है।
मौसम विज्ञान एजेंसियों का अनुमान है कि कम वर्षा के कारण मध्य और दक्षिणी वियतनाम में नदियों का प्रवाह कई वर्षों के औसत से कम रहेगा। यह एक ऐसा कारक है जो मेकांग डेल्टा में खारे पानी के घुसपैठ के खतरे को बढ़ाता है, जिससे यह कई वर्षों के औसत से अधिक गंभीर और पहले हो सकता है।
एल नीनो एक ऐसी घटना है जिसमें मध्य और पूर्वी भूमध्यरेखीय प्रशांत महासागर में समुद्री जल की सतह की परत असामान्य रूप से गर्म हो जाती है, जिससे वैश्विक स्तर पर मौसम और जलवायु के पैटर्न में बदलाव आता है।

Public Works Authority Ashghal has completed a pilot of cool pavement on roads in Qatar. The authority announced the work on 19 August 2019. An asphalt-cooling material was applied to up to 200 metres of vehicle lanes on Abdullah bin Jassim Street, beside Souq Waqif, and to 200 metres of pedestrian and bicycle paths in front of Katara, the Cultural Village. According to an official from the Public Works Authority ('Ashghal') in Qatar, conventional asphalt absorbs up to 80 to 95% of sunlight, while the new coating reflects about 50%. Sensors will compare its temperature with conventional asphalt over an 18-month study, carried out with the Japanese company Oriental.
Why is Qatar painting some roads blue instead of black
The pilot used an asphalt-cooling material on parts of Abdullah bin Jassim Street, next to Souq Waqif. The authority says it was applied to vehicle lanes over a length of up to 200 metres. The same material was also tested on 200 metres of pedestrian and bicycle paths in front of Katara, the Cultural Village.
The road was opened to traffic so that testing could begin. The authority says the aim is to measure how effective the material is and to judge whether the experiment succeeds. It adds that the result could lead to formal use of the material across the road network in the State of Qatar.
How long will Qatar’s blue road study last
Ashghal says the study will last 18 months. Based on the outcome, the authority will decide whether the pilot has succeeded and how widely the material could be applied. The announcement says road experts and contractors have installed special devices and sensors on the pilot sections.
According to Ashghal, these sensors measure how well the material reduces asphalt temperature and compare the results with conventional asphalt. The authority says the work was carried out in cooperation with the Japanese company Oriental, which it describes as one of the leading companies in implementing this technology.
Why does conventional asphalt absorb up to 95% of sunlight
Ashghal explains that conventional asphalt contributes to rising temperatures because it absorbs up to 80 to 95% of sunlight. Cool pavement, the authority says, reflects ultraviolet rays and absorbs less solar radiation. Ashghal adds that this can have a positive effect on overall temperature reduction, given the size of the areas covered by conventional asphalt.
On the specification, Ashghal says cooled paving material can be made from traditional paving materials such as concrete. The authority says the new coating on the concrete asphalt layer reflects "about 50% of sunlight". It states that the coating consists of four layers: a primary layer, followed by three consecutive layers that reduce the heat absorbed from solar radiation.
How does Qatar’s cool pavement improve road safety
The announcement says a protective material has been applied to the ground markings. According to Ashghal, this shields the markings from contact with vehicles and increases their lifespan. The authority links cool pavement to energy efficiency and says research by environment and sustainability experts suggests it can reduce overall temperature and, as a result, emissions.
Ashghal also cites research suggesting that cool paving material reduces heat-related illnesses and slows the formation of smog. The authority says it can improve pedestrians' ability to use the road and promote traffic safety, because light-coloured pavements reflect street lights and car headlights better and make vehicles more visible to drivers. In addition, Ashghal says that lowering air temperatures in residential areas can slow the chemical reactions in the atmosphere that cause smog.

CHENNAI: A 13-year-old deaf boy crossing the railway tracks near his house at Mathur Colony near Tiruttani was killed by an oncoming train on Thursday morning. The boy had gone out to relieve himself in the open because there was no toilet in the government-built house his family was living in. Police sources said he may not have heard the approaching train due to a hearing impairment he had had since birth.
The deceased was identified as K Surya Prakash, a Class 8 student at the Government Middle School in Mathur Panchayat. His father, T Kalidasan, is a daily-wage worker and his mother is a homemaker. He also has an elder sister.
Speaking to TNIE, Kalidasan said the family lived in a government-built house without a toilet and had initially petitioned the government for one but had received no response. The family was left with no choice but to use vacant plots in the surrounding area to relieve themselves. “My son sometimes uses the railway tracks and sometimes other places to relieve himself. It is not just our house, several houses in this panchayat do not have toilets,” he said.
When contacted, the block development officer for Mathur Panchayat, Selvi, said toilets were generally constructed for group houses under a government scheme. “I’m not aware of how the toilets were left out in this particular case. I will look into the matter,” she said.
Police sources said Surya Prakash had gone alone to the railway tracks around 7.50 am to relieve himself and was crossing the single track when the train hit him, killing him on the spot.
The Arakkonam GRP sent the body to Tiruvallur Government Medical College Hospital for postmortem, after which his relatives took the body home, sources said. A case has been registered under Section 194 of the BNSS, and further probe is under way.

title: Mumbai Heatwave: Why October Temperatures Have Soared - Urban Acres

full_text:
Mumbai’s record October heatwave is not being driven by one local factor. The city’s unusually high temperatures are emerging from the interaction of an early monsoon withdrawal, dry northwesterly winds, a regional anticyclonic system and the delayed arrival of the sea breeze that normally moderates daytime heat. The result is a coastal city experiencing temperatures more commonly associated with a sharper post-monsoon transition.
The India Meteorological Department has placed Mumbai, Thane and Palghar under a heatwave because the city’s temperatures have risen well above the October norm. Mumbai’s Santacruz observatory recorded 38 degrees Celsius on October 11, 4.9 degrees above normal. That was the hottest October day recorded there since 2015, when the temperature reached 38.6 degrees on October 17. The suburban station then recorded 38.2 degrees the following day and 38 degrees the day after that.
Those figures are significant because 38 degrees is not a routine October temperature for Mumbai. Apart from 2015, the city had reached that mark only once in the previous 11 years, when temperatures touched 38 degrees in October 2018. The sequence of high readings therefore points to an unusual heat spell rather than a single isolated afternoon.
What makes the episode particularly important for understanding Mumbai is that the immediate cause lies partly outside the city. An anticyclonic system over southwest Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat has produced clockwise air movement, with winds reaching Mumbai from northwesterly and westerly directions. These winds have travelled from areas including Rajasthan, bringing dry and warm air into the Mumbai region.
Mahesh Palawat of Skymet Weather Services explained that the northerly winds are dry and warm, raising temperatures while delaying the sea breeze. That local breeze is crucial to Mumbai’s daily cooling cycle. When it arrives later than usual, the city loses one of its most important natural mechanisms for moderating daytime heat. The absence of cloud cover has also allowed more direct heating.
This is the first structural lesson from the current heatwave: a coastal location does not provide permanent protection from extreme heat. Mumbai’s relationship with the Arabian Sea usually creates a cooling influence through the sea breeze, but that influence depends on the prevailing wind pattern and the wider atmospheric setup. When dry continental air moves in and the sea breeze is delayed, the city’s coastal advantage is weakened.
The second factor is timing. Mumbai is accustomed to what is locally known as October heat after the southwest monsoon withdraws. During this period, the sun’s rays are less slanted and can produce stronger heating. But this year, the monsoon withdrew on October 3, earlier than the normal withdrawal date of October 10 or 11. That exposed the city to post-monsoon conditions sooner than usual.
An early withdrawal does not automatically produce a heatwave. In this case, however, it created the conditions for high temperatures to persist while regional wind systems reinforced the warming. The absence of cloud cover then made the heat feel more direct. The episode illustrates how several ordinary seasonal processes can combine to create an exceptional urban temperature event.
The report also identifies a possible contribution from a powerful El Niño weather pattern. Meteorologist Mahesh Palawat said El Niño may be one factor behind the early and warmer October heat this year. The supplied evidence does not establish that El Niño alone caused Mumbai’s heatwave. Instead, it places the current event within a wider atmospheric pattern that may be amplifying local and regional conditions.
That distinction matters. Heat events in cities are often described through a single headline number, such as the maximum temperature recorded at an observatory. But the lived experience of heat depends on timing, humidity, wind, cloud cover and the duration of the spell. The current episode combines high daytime temperatures with hot and humid conditions, while the delayed sea breeze removes part of the relief normally available later in the day.
Mumbai’s observatories provide the clearest evidence of the event’s intensity. Santacruz recorded 38 degrees on October 11, followed by 38.2 degrees at the suburban station on October 12 and 38 degrees the next day. Colaba and the suburban areas may not experience identical conditions, but both locations are part of the city’s heat-monitoring system. The difference between island-city and suburban readings is relevant because Mumbai is not climatically uniform, even within a compact metropolitan area.
The heatwave classification covering Mumbai, Thane and Palghar also shows that the event is regional rather than confined to one neighbourhood or one observatory. The same broad atmospheric conditions are affecting neighbouring districts, while Raigad and Ratnagiri have separately received a yellow alert because of the possibility of thunderstorms and gusty winds. This combination of heat, changing winds and possible storms reflects a transitional period in the post-monsoon atmosphere.
The institutional response is centred on monitoring and forecasting. The IMD has issued the heatwave classification and provided the forecast for changing conditions later in the week. The meteorological explanation from Skymet adds detail on the wind pattern and the delayed sea breeze. Together, these inputs show how urban heat information is assembled: observatory readings establish the anomaly, official warnings identify the level of concern, and meteorological analysis explains the atmospheric mechanism.
The expected change in weather also demonstrates why forecasts need to be read as a sequence rather than as a single temperature prediction. The current heat spell is likely to continue until the weekend. From October 17, Mumbai and neighbouring districts may see cloudy skies and one or two spells of rainfall with thunderstorms. A change in wind direction could bring moist south-easterly winds, with maximum temperatures potentially falling to about 35 degrees in suburban Mumbai and 34 degrees in Colaba.
These projected values would represent relief from the 38-degree readings, but they would not mean that the city had returned to a uniformly cool condition. The forecast describes a transition from intense heat towards cloud and possible rainfall. It also carries different implications across the region: Mumbai and Thane had not received alerts at the time of the report, while Raigad and Ratnagiri were under a yellow alert for possible thunderstorms and gusty winds.
The broader urban question is how Mumbai prepares for heat that does not fit the city’s traditional image of a monsoon-dominated coastal climate. The current evidence does not establish a long-term trend by itself, nor does it prove that every future October will resemble this one. It does, however, show that heat risk can rise quickly when seasonal timing, regional circulation and local cooling mechanisms change at the same time.
For residents, the practical significance is that the city’s heat conditions cannot be assessed only by looking at whether the monsoon has ended or whether Mumbai is near the sea. The timing of withdrawal, the direction of incoming winds, cloud cover and the arrival of the sea breeze all influence how heat is experienced. For city institutions, the episode underlines the importance of treating heat as a regional atmospheric event with local urban consequences.
What the evidence confirms is clear: Mumbai’s October heatwave was marked by temperatures significantly above normal, an early monsoon withdrawal, dry and warm winds from the northwestern sector, reduced cloud cover and delayed sea-breeze relief. The immediate forecast pointed to possible improvement after the weekend as winds changed and rainfall returned. What remains less certain is the precise contribution of the wider El Niño pattern. The next important milestone is the forecast change expected from October 17, when cloud cover, thunderstorms and post-monsoon showers could begin easing the heat.

UCLA left students in dorms sweltering. The university must revise its heat wave plan.
Sproul Hall is pictured. Columnist Ruby Galbraith argues that UCLA must do more to provide safe places for students amid extreme heat crises. (Crystal Tompkins/Daily Bruin senior staff)
Jade Fraser woke up every two hours from the heat last week.
“I can’t sleep,” said Fraser, a first-year human biology and society student who lives in Dykstra Hall, which doesn’t have air conditioning. “I have a lot of headaches and I think I’m dehydrating a lot.”
Fraser’s story is not singular. Students reported experiencing health issues after temperatures in Westwood reached up to 101 degrees during last week’s heat wave, which triggered Stage 1 of UCLA’s Campus Cooling Response Plan.
Yet this plan, outlined on the UCLA Facilities website, contains no information about protecting students in university housing from extreme temperatures. As campus temperatures climb once again, UCLA needs to ensure students have a safe place to rest and study during extreme heat events.
This includes dedicating spaces for cooling before heat waves, repairing broken air conditioning and considering implementing air conditioning across all UCLA Housing.
[Related: Students in dorms without AC find their rooms unbearable amid heat wave]
Many on-campus residences do not have air conditioning, including Dykstra Hall, Hedrick Hall, Rieber Hall, Sproul Hall, Hitch Suites and Saxon Suites.
On Oct. 5, UCLA Housing announced it would open the air-conditioned De Neve Plaza Room for students to use. Residential Life hoped the additional spaces would provide students a place to cool down and study, said Lauren Han, an employee of the Sunset Village Learning Center.
Residential Life’s effort to improve student comfort is admirable, but should be part of a detailed, institutionalized plan rather than a hasty mid-heat-wave decision.
Installing air conditioning in all residential buildings is the most ideal outcome – even if that strategy comes with a litany of financial and logistical challenges.
With the progression of climate change, extreme heat will likely become an increasing reality for students. Installing AC must be considered by UCLA administrators, without placing additional financial strain on students.
In the meantime, the university can take smaller, more realistic steps to promote heat safety for current students. Housing should create a plan outlining air-conditioned spaces it can open for students during heat waves, as well as designate staff to run these spaces overnight. Even a fan rental process could help students mitigate some symptoms of extreme heat.
These relief efforts are a necessary addition to the UCLA Campus Cooling Response Plan and should be easily accessible to students living in university housing.
Heat is still a problem even in residences equipped with AC. Emily Ruby, a fourth-year political science and public affairs student, said the air conditioning unit in her Gayley Court apartment has been broken since she moved in.
“I’m on medication that makes me susceptible to heat stroke,” Ruby said.
Despite attempts at resolving the issue with UCLA Housing, she alleged it has not been responsive to her requests. UCLA Media Relations did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
UCLA needs to prioritize fixing its current air conditioning system to ensure students get the maintenance they need during extreme heat events.
For students without underlying health conditions, the heat wave may have just been a sweltering inconvenience. For others, the weather was significant enough to impact their academic performance.
Grace Tan, a first-year physics student who lives in Hedrick Hall without AC, said she had a hard time sleeping during the heat wave, impacting her concentration in class.
UCLA residential spaces should provide students the conditions they need to succeed. Now more than ever, extreme heat will factor into that equation.
In the Oct. 5 email, UCLA Housing reminded students that they can open their windows to increase airflow.
But when temperatures reach 101 degrees, the health and academic success of the student body depends on the university creating a better plan than that.

Extreme Heat Pushes Germany’s 2026 Grape Harvest Into August
Growers say overlapping ripening compressed the season, cut must volumes, forced crews into dawn or overnight shifts.
Thursday, October 15, 2026
Germany’s 2026 grape harvest began in August in several wine regions, one of the earliest starts many producers say they have ever seen, as extreme summer heat pushed different grape varieties to ripen almost at the same time and forced crews to work at dawn, and in some places at night, to protect both fruit quality and workers.
According to a report from Slow Food Deutschland, many wineries again recorded the earliest harvest in their history. At some estates, all of the grapes had been brought in and pressed by the middle of September. Growers said the pace was unusually fast because varieties that would normally be harvested weeks apart were ready within a narrow window from late August to early September.
The early harvest followed a summer marked by record temperatures and little rain. But growers and wine industry officials said the crop was helped by high winter moisture and a mostly wet May, which prevented more severe drought stress in many vineyards. Even after another heat wave in September, many vines still had enough water, the report said.
The combination produced a complicated vintage. Growers described the fruit as very healthy and fully ripe, with small berries and concentrated flavors. At the same time, they reported low juice yields from the press, meaning the volume of must, the freshly pressed grape juice used to make wine, was lower than the appearance of the crop had suggested.
Hansjörg Aldinger of the Aldinger winery in Fellbach, in Württemberg, told Slow Food Deutschland that an early harvest had become necessary to preserve acidity. He said his estate started picking on Aug. 18, three days earlier than in the already early 2018 vintage. By mid-September, the winery had finished processing all of its grapes.
That concern over acidity has become central for German producers as temperatures rise. In a typical year, growers monitor both ripeness and Oechsle, the German measure of grape sugar. In 2026, several growers said they were not worried about reaching sugar levels. The bigger question was how to keep enough freshness in the grapes while avoiding overripe fruit and excessively heavy wines.
Despite the heat and dryness, growers said acidity held up better than expected in many places because the small berries concentrated not only sugars and flavors but also acids. That balance may prove important for Germany’s wine sector, where accelerated ripening and lower must yields can affect both the style and supply of finished wines. Smaller volumes of juice could limit output for some bottlings, while the need to harvest earlier or overnight may increase labor and cellar pressures for producers and, potentially, reshape supply for the broader beverage trade.
In the Kaiserstuhl region of Baden, Alexander Schneider of Weingut Schneider in Endingen said the 2026 crop combined small quantities, small berries and very healthy, ripe fruit. Slow Food Deutschland quoted him saying the harvest team often had to stop by 2 p.m. because of the heat. The report said the southwest of Germany recorded more than 60 days above 30 degrees Celsius, or 86 degrees Fahrenheit, this year.
For crews in the vineyards, the conditions were physically demanding. Ernst Büscher of the German Wine Institute said some regions harvested at night again this year. Growers said early starts were necessary so workers could be in the vineyards shortly after sunrise. The shift in working hours is one of the clearest operational changes linked to hotter summers.
Philipp Kuhn, a winemaker in the northern Palatinate, used unusually strong language to describe the fruit. Slow Food Deutschland quoted him as saying it was “as if a UFO had landed,” adding that in 35 years of experience he had never seen grapes so perfect and so uniform. Such assessments reflect the quality of the fruit, but they do not change the fact that juice extraction was weaker than many producers expected.
Hermann Deppisch, a Slow Wine producer in Franconia, said the crop initially looked larger on the vine than it turned out to be in the press. He said that in the end, “very little came out.” The reason, he said, was the year’s high skin-to-juice ratio: thick or abundant skins, but relatively little liquid inside. For winemakers, that can reduce volume while increasing aroma and structure.
That profile is likely to favor red wines in particular. Slow Food Deutschland said growers expect concentrated reds from the 2026 vintage, with deep color, strong aroma and solid tannin structure because much of a grape’s flavor compounds are found in the skin. Deppisch also said Sylvaner handled the heat relatively well.
In the vineyards, hotter conditions also changed standard growing practices. Defoliation, the removal of leaves around the grape zone to increase sun exposure, was largely skipped this year, according to the report. Instead, growers tried to shield bunches from too much direct sunlight and removed leaves, if at all, mainly on the shaded side to improve airflow without increasing the risk of sunburn.
Another unusual feature of the vintage was how little fruit had to be discarded at sorting tables. Growers said the grapes were largely free of rot. The main fruit removed before pressing consisted of very small, raisin-like berries, which were screened out to keep sugar levels from climbing too high and to avoid dried-fruit flavors in the finished wines.
In eastern Germany, the two wine regions of Saale-Unstrut and Saxony also reported strong fruit quality. Klaus Zimmerling, an organic grower in Dresden-Pillnitz, began harvest on Sept. 3 and completed the entire picking season in about two and a half weeks without weather interruptions, the report said. But he described the volume as very low, at only 30 hectoliters per hectare.
Zimmerling also reported an unusually early harvest for Gewürztraminer, a grape that is usually picked much later. This year, he brought it in at the start of September, about seven weeks ahead of its normal schedule. The report described that kind of shift as another sign of how quickly German viticulture is changing.
Growers interviewed by Slow Food Deutschland contrasted the current harvest with much cooler decades in the past, when late October snow and unripe grapes were still possible. Today, many face the opposite problem: heat, drought, rising sugar levels and, increasingly, the need to add acidity in the cellar to keep wines balanced.

By Rafiq Vayani
KARACHI: The Karachi Press Club Environment Committee and the Climate Action Center Karachi (CAC) held a joint training session for journalists and media professionals titled “Extreme Heat, Climate Change & Karachi” at the Karachi Press Club today. The session was among the Committee’s early initiatives and drew a full house.
Led by Yasir Husain, Director of the Climate Action Center Karachi, the three-hour session aimed to help reporters cover extreme heat more accurately and in more depth. It was attended by Fahmida Yusuf, Secretary of the KPC Environment Committee, Fazil Jamili, President of the Karachi Press Club, and Aslam Khan, Secretary of the Karachi Press Club.
Speaking about the Committee’s decision to organize the session, Fahmida Yusuf said: “An initiative like the KPC environment committee has never been undertaken, but such is the crisis that we at the Karachi Press Club felt the need to step forward and provide a platform to a much needed conversation, which is how we ultimately came to arrange this session.”
The sole speaker, Mr. Husain began with the basics, explaining how humidity changes the way heat affects the body. For example, an air temperature of 35°C with 70% humidity can feel closer to 50°C. He then covered the role of El Niño, the seasonal pattern of heat and humidity in Karachi, and the links between extreme heat, water stress, agriculture and the shrinking Indus Delta.
“Climate change is a corporate term. Change can be good or bad. We are in a state of climate emergency, this is a climate crisis,” Mr. Husain said. “Unfortunately, we have not seen dialog or response to match the scale and magnitude of the emergency, which is why we held this training in the first place.”
Participants also reviewed research on the city. This included heat-vulnerability maps from the Karachi Climate Action Plan and thermal imaging of buildings by Dr. Jameel Kazmi. They also discussed Aga Khan University’s heat-adaptation trials in Karachi and Matiari, which test reflective roof coatings, ventilation and roof shading. Karachi Urban Lab data shows daytime temperatures in the city rising by 1.6°C and nighttime temperatures by 2.4°C over 60 years.
The session also addressed energy poverty, noting that some Karachi localities face up to 10 hours of daily load-shedding, which leaves residents with less cooling during heatwaves. It looked at energy-efficient building design, including ECBC 2023 and SBCA bylaws, before turning to the Karachi Cooling Plan. Developed with PMD, the health sector, civil society, academia and urban experts, the plan includes strengthened early warning systems, 10,000 urban forests, heat resilience in the Karachi Master Plan 2047, heat-ready healthcare, community cooling centers and affordable cooling solutions.
Journalists asked enthusiastic questions towards the end, and Mr. Husain answered them at length, on topics including heatwaves and public health and the impact on outdoor workers, women, children and the elderly.
The Karachi Press Club Environment Committee and the Climate Action Center said they will continue working together to strengthen climate reporting in Pakistan.

KwaZulu-Natal communities are being urged to prepare for potentially severe heatwaves, prolonged dry spells and water shortages, with below-normal rainfall forecast for the province in the coming months.
The South African Weather Service (Saws) seasonal outlook indicates that KZN could experience below-normal rainfall between October and December 2026, with dry conditions potentially continuing into March 2027.

Above-normal temperatures and an increased risk of severe and frequent heatwaves are also forecast.
KZN Co-operative Governance and Traditional Affairs (Cogta) MEC Reverend Thulasizwe Buthelezi has called on residents, farmers and businesses to take precautions as the province prepares for the possible effects of El Niño.
The weather phenomenon, associated with warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, can influence weather patterns and increase the likelihood of drier conditions in parts of southern Africa.
Potential consequences include water shortages, veld and forest fires, reduced agricultural production, livestock losses and increased pressure on health services.
Children, older people and residents of informal settlements are particularly vulnerable to extreme heat, while prolonged dry conditions during the planting season could threaten crop yields and food security.

Water conservation and disaster preparedness
Through the Provincial Disaster Management Centre (PDMC), Cogta is co-ordinating preparations with municipalities and departments responsible for health, agriculture, water and sanitation, environmental affairs and social development.
“The PDMC will closely monitor drought indicators and co-ordinate preparedness planning across the province,” Buthelezi said.
“We are engaging municipalities to address water leaks, strengthen water conservation measures and develop contingency plans to maintain water supplies.”
He said water services authorities must prioritise conservation and ensure that drought response measures are in place.
The Department of Water and Sanitation will monitor dam levels and support drought response measures, while the Department of Agriculture will advise farmers on climate-smart practices and drought-resistant crops.
Farmers and residents urged to take precautions
Buthelezi urged farmers to monitor livestock closely and take steps to protect animals from heat stress and possible water shortages.

Residents were also urged to use water responsibly, avoid activities that could trigger veld and forest fires, and take precautions during periods of extreme heat.
“We will work with all social partners, technical experts, municipalities and Amakhosi to ensure that communities throughout KwaZulu-Natal receive timely information and practical guidance,” he said.
“Disaster preparedness is a collective responsibility, and early action can help reduce the impact of these conditions on our people and their livelihoods.”
Buthelezi called on the public to follow official weather advisories, heed warnings and take precautions to protect their families, livestock and property.

A fire danger warning covers parts of Zululand, uMzinyathi, Amajuba, uThukela, uMkhanyakude and King Cetshwayo as hot, dry weather raises the risk of fires.
Residents in northern KZN have been urged to avoid starting open fires due to dry, windy conditions.
A fire danger warning was in place for the region on Friday, with a heatwave expected to persist until Saturday.
-Avoid outdoor activities-
South African Weather Service forecaster Ayanda Ntsele urged residents to stay hydrated, avoid strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest parts of the day and take extra care of children, the elderly and pets.
“Those hot, coupled with dry conditions, will improve the chances of fires developing and spreading in parts of Zululand, uMzinyathi, Amajuba, uThukela, uMkhanyakude, as well as parts of King Cetshway.”
She said the weather isn't unusual as the province moves into summer.
“And moving into summer, seasonal focus indicates that you are expecting above normal maximum temperatures.”
Ntsele said cooler conditions are expected to bring some relief on Sunday.
-Hottest year-
An intensifying El Niño pattern set an all-time temperature high in a key Pacific zone in September and could help make this year the hottest year on record globally, the director of the EU's climate monitor said Monday.
Global forecasters have been warning for months that this El Niño would likely become the strongest ever observed, and the latest record has tumbled even before the episode's expected peak later this year.
The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Niño, temporarily raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming.
The Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures in a tell-tale El Niño monitoring region of the Pacific, known as Niño3.4, had reached an "all-time high" of 29.70 °C last month.
This exceeded the peak temperatures of previously strong El Niño events of 1982/1983, 1997/1998 and 2015/2016, the EU monitor said.
This year's El Niño, which emerged in June, is "very exceptional", but it is too early to say whether it is the strongest ever observed, Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo told AFP.
As climate change raises ocean temperatures, recent El Niño events may appear stronger than past ones, complicating historical comparisons.

Telangana’s peak power demand hits all-time high of 20,003 MW
Telangana’s peak electricity demand reached a record 20,003 MW on October 15, while daily consumption climbed to 334.54 million units. Rising agricultural, domestic, commercial and industrial needs are putting pressure on utilities, which are procuring additional power and monitoring supply.
Hyderabad: Telangana’s peak electricity demand touched an all-time high of 20,003 MW on October 15, surpassing the previous financial year’s record of 18,548 MW by 1,455 MW.
The State’s daily electricity consumption also reached 334.54 million units (MU) on Thursday. Between October 1 and 15, Telangana recorded an average peak demand of 19,289 MW and average daily consumption of 321.34 MU.
The rising demand, driven by agricultural, domestic, commercial, IT and industrial requirements, has put additional pressure on power utilities to ensure uninterrupted supply.
TGSPDCL records higher consumption
Within the Telangana State Southern Power Distribution Company Limited (TGSPDCL) jurisdiction, peak demand reached 12,281 MW on October 15, while daily consumption stood at 228.14 MU. On Friday, it increased to 12,532 MW at 12.01, officials said.
GHMC area sees rising demand
The Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) area recorded a peak demand of 4,220 MW at 6.19 pm on October 15. Daily electricity consumption in the area touched 88.22 MU on October 9.
The peak demand was significantly higher than the 3,552 MW recorded in October last year. Rising domestic and commercial consumption, IT operations, industrial activity and increased use of cooling appliances amid hot and humid weather have contributed to the growing demand.
TGSPDCL Chairman and Managing Director Jitesh V. Patil said the power supply was being managed to meet the growing requirements of agricultural, domestic, commercial, IT and industrial consumers.
He said agricultural consumption was rising, particularly due to increased dependence on borewells and the use of water-pumping motors amid declining groundwater levels. The utilities were procuring additional power and taking steps to enhance generation capacity to meet the demand, he added.
In a statement, Patil appealed to consumers to use electricity judiciously and avoid wastage. He also stressed the need to conserve water and adopt energy-efficient practices, including switching off electrical appliances when not in use.
Meanwhile, officials are inspecting power supply conditions, groundwater levels, borewell availability, irrigation motor operations and crop conditions in rural areas. They have been directed to address problems such as supply interruptions, faulty agricultural motors, damaged service wires and transformer failures promptly.
Officials have also been instructed to remain accessible to farmers in the fields and give priority to complaints related to agricultural power supply.

Executive Summary for the Visayas Power Grid Yellow Alert
The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) has placed the Visayas power grid under a yellow alert on 16 October due to reduced available generation capacity and limited electricity imports from the Mindanao grid. The alert is expected to apply during the evening period, with reports indicating a window of approximately 1700 to 1900 hours local time. Available capacity is estimated at 2,545 megawatts (MW), against projected peak demand of 2,471 MW. Although supply is expected to exceed demand, the operating reserve is insufficient to meet the grid’s required contingency margin. The shortfall is linked to the unavailability of Panay Energy Development Corporation Unit 3 and KEPCO SPC Power Corporation Unit 1, alongside restricted power imports due to outages and maintenance affecting generating units in Mindanao. Eighteen other power plants are reportedly operating at reduced capacity, leaving approximately 657.1 MW of generating capacity unavailable. A yellow alert does not automatically mean a blackout will occur, but it signals reduced resilience if another generating unit or supply source becomes unavailable.
What is Risk Analysis in the Context of Critical Infrastructure Events
Critical infrastructure event risk analysis assesses whether available generation and reserve capacity can maintain reliable supply if demand rises or an unexpected outage occurs. The principal concerns include reduced reserve capacity, potential supply interruptions, impacts on business continuity and critical services.
Known Hotspots and Sensitive Areas
High Impact
- Electricity-dependent industrial and commercial facilities across the Visayas: Facilities that require uninterrupted power, including manufacturing operations, cold-storage sites and data-dependent services, have heightened exposure if the grid experiences further stress.
- Essential infrastructure: Hospitals, water-supply systems, telecommunications facilities and emergency services should verify backup power availability and readiness.
Medium Impact
- Commercial centers and retail businesses: Retail outlets, offices, hotels and restaurants may experience disruption if an unplanned outage occurs, particularly during evening peak demand.
- Small and medium-sized enterprises: Businesses without generators or backup power may be more vulnerable to interruptions affecting payment systems, refrigeration, lighting and customer service.
- Power-dependent logistics: Warehousing and distribution operations may need contingency arrangements for refrigeration, security systems and electrically powered equipment.
Low Impact
- Facilities with tested backup systems: Businesses with reliable generators, battery storage or uninterruptible power supplies may be better positioned to maintain essential operations during a short interruption.
- Operations with flexible electricity demand: Facilities able to defer non-essential energy use may have greater flexibility during periods of grid stress.
Impact on Transportation and Services
- Electricity supply: The immediate concern is reduced grid reserve capacity. The yellow alert indicates limited contingency protection rather than a confirmed supply deficit.
- Telecommunications: Mobile networks and communications infrastructure may be affected if a power interruption outlasts local backup capacity.
- Water and public utilities: Electrically powered pumping, treatment and distribution facilities should verify backup arrangements.
- Commercial operations: An outage could disrupt point-of-sale systems, refrigeration, lighting, production and digital services.
- Transportation: Airports, ports and electrically dependent transport systems may be exposed to localized service disruption if their power supply is affected.
- Emergency services: Critical facilities should prioritize continuity of essential systems and ensure backup power arrangements are operational.

A western disturbance changed weather conditions in more than seven districts of Rajasthan on Thursday, bringing cloudy skies, rain and hailstorms in some areas, with Gajsinghpur in Sri Ganganagar recording the highest rainfall of 55 mm and the Suratgarh area experiencing heavy hailstorms. A yellow alert has been issued for heavy rain, thunderstorms and hailstorms in seven districts, including Jaipur, for Friday.
Light clouds remained in the sky over Jaipur throughout Thursday. After noon, light rain and drizzle occurred at a few places in Jaipur’s rural areas. The Jaipur airport recorded 0.5 mm of rainfall, while Chaksu received 6 mm. Cold winds made the weather colder in Jaipur.
Barmer recorded the highest temperature in the state on Thursday, at 40.5 degrees Celsius. Jaisalmer recorded 39.4 degrees, Phalodi 38.4, Jodhpur 38.9, Chittorgarh 38.2 and Sirohi 38.5 degrees Celsius, with relatively warm conditions prevailing in these areas.
Rain and hail damage crops in Sri Ganganagar
Rain occurred in parts of Udaipur, Sikar, Jaipur, Tonk, Alwar, Bharatpur, Sawai Madhopur, Hanumangarh, Churu and Sri Ganganagar over the past 24 hours. Sri Ganganagar experienced heavy stormy rain late on the night of 14 October.
More than 2 inches of rain was recorded in Gajsinghpur, while heavy hail fell in the Suratgarh area. Rain and hail damaged crops that had been cut and were lying in fields in these areas.
Jurohra in Bharatpur receives 45 mm of rain
Weather conditions changed in Sikar, Jaipur, Alwar, Bharatpur, Dausa, Sawai Madhopur and surrounding areas, bringing rain accompanied by thunder and lightning. Strong, cold winds and light to moderate rain occurred in Sikar and Alwar after Thursday afternoon.
Patan in Sikar recorded 10 mm of rainfall, Tijara near Alwar received 5 mm, Bharatpur 17 mm, Jurohra in Bharatpur district 45 mm, Kaman 26 mm, Pahari 28 mm and Kumher 22 mm.
Temperatures fall by 5 degrees in Sri Ganganagar, Churu and Hanumangarh
Rain and hail brought down temperatures across districts, including Churu, Hanumangarh and Sri Ganganagar. As a result, the cold intensified both at night and during the day.
Hanumangarh recorded its coldest day on Thursday, with a maximum temperature of 28.1 degrees Celsius. Other areas also experienced cooler daytime conditions, with Pilani recording 28.9 degrees, Sri Ganganagar 30.4, Churu 32.6, Alwar 33 and Jhunjhunu 31.3 degrees Celsius.
Maximum temperatures fell by up to 5 degrees Celsius in Sri Ganganagar, Churu and Hanumangarh.
Chaksu in Jaipur receives 6 mm of rain, temperatures suddenly drop in the evening
Light clouds remained over the state capital, Jaipur, throughout the day yesterday. This weakened the sunshine and brought down the maximum temperature. After noon, light rain and drizzle occurred at a few places in Jaipur’s rural areas. Jaipur airport recorded 0.5 mm of rainfall, while Chaksu received 6 mm. Strong, cold winds swept through Jaipur city in the late evening, causing temperatures to drop suddenly.
Jaipur recorded a maximum temperature of 34.1 degrees Celsius and a minimum of 24.2 degrees Celsius yesterday. The Meteorological Department has issued a yellow alert for cloudy conditions and light rain or drizzle at isolated places in Jaipur today as well.

Heavy rain brought traffic across Delhi to a crawl on Thursday, with waterlogging and packed junctions disrupting movement from India Gate and ITO to Mandi House, south Delhi, Model Town and Okhla Phase 1 as the India Meteorological Department issued a red alert for the capital.
Long queues of cars, buses and three-wheelers were reported on several stretches, while commuters sought intervention from the traffic police as rainfall worsened congestion on already busy roads. The city remained overcast through much of the day, with dark clouds, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds forecast under the IMD alert.
At Mandi House Circle, vehicles were seen packed tightly together. Commuters claimed on social media that traffic personnel were not present to regulate the flow. Near India Gate, one commuter reported that traffic had remained stuck for nearly 30 minutes.
Congestion was also reported on the Vikas Marg-ITO stretch and on roads linking ITO with the Supreme Court and Bharat Mandapam. Heavy traffic was seen near the Supreme Court as well, adding pressure to a network of roads serving central Delhi’s administrative and commercial areas.
In south Delhi, vehicles queued from the Chirag Delhi red light towards IIT Delhi and Hauz Khas. Commuters also reported heavy traffic near the Ashram flyover exit towards Sarai Kale Khan and Sunlight Colony. Around Okhla Phase 1, congestion was allegedly worsened by encroachments and construction materials stored on footpaths, according to the report.
Waterlogging was reported near Mandi House and Geeta Colony, while traffic snarls were also seen around Palam and AIIMS. In Model Town, waterlogging coincided with end-of-school-hour traffic, worsening delays for commuters and school vehicles.
The traffic police responded to at least one complaint by saying that the matter had been forwarded to the concerned traffic circle for action. The IMD’s red alert covers moderate rain, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds in Delhi, keeping the possibility of further disruption active as traffic authorities respond to affected stretches.

Delhi recorded rainfall on Thursday that lowered daytime temperatures by four to six degrees Celsius and improved air quality, while the India Meteorological Department issued a red alert warning of moderate to heavy showers, lightning and squally winds across the Capital.
Maximum temperatures settled between 27 and 28 degrees Celsius at major weather stations, according to the IMD bulletin. Safdarjung, Delhi’s base station, recorded 15.9 mm of rainfall, while the Ridge recorded the highest precipitation among the listed stations at 25.2 mm. Lodi Road received 20 mm, Palam recorded 11.2 mm and Ayanagar 7.2 mm.
The rainfall also brought a measurable improvement in Delhi’s air quality. The city’s air quality index stood at 149 on Thursday, down from 181 a day earlier. While the change coincided with the rain and strong winds, the supplied weather report does not provide a separate assessment of how long the improvement is expected to last.
The weather shift was linked by officials to multiple systems affecting north India. These included a Western Disturbance persisting as a cyclonic circulation over north Punjab and adjoining areas, an upper-air cyclonic circulation over south Haryana and neighbouring regions, and a low-pressure area extending from northeast Uttar Pradesh to the East-Central Arabian Sea through East Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.
Strong surface winds swept across Delhi at speeds of 20-30 kmph, with gusts reaching 50-60 kmph, IMD officials said. The combination of rain, lightning and gusty winds presents an immediate operational challenge for road users and outdoor activity, although the supplied report does not record any disruption, damage or casualty linked to the weather.
The Regional Meteorological Centre forecast generally cloudy skies overnight, with further spells of light rain, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds of 40-50 kmph, gusting up to 60 kmph. Similar conditions were expected to continue through Friday morning and noon before easing.
The weather department said skies are likely to clear towards the weekend, with daytime temperatures expected to rise gradually to 31-33 degrees Celsius. The forecast makes Friday’s rain and wind conditions the next immediate milestone for Delhi residents and city authorities.
